lesson.title: Linear Equations: The Algebra of Straight Lines
lesson.summary: A linear equation in two variables describes every point on a straight line, and writing it in slope intercept form, y = mx + b, packs the line's entire steepness and starting position into just two numbers.
lesson.body:
The equations you solved in the last chapter had one variable and one specific numerical answer, like x = 5. A linear equation with two variables, x and y, works differently: instead of a single solution, it has infinitely many solution pairs (x, y), and when you plot every one of those pairs on a coordinate grid, they line up perfectly to form a straight line. The equation is not asking 'what one number works,' it is describing an entire relationship between two quantities, which is what makes it so useful for modeling real situations like cost versus time or distance versus speed.

The most useful way to write a linear equation is slope intercept form, y = mx + b. Here, b is the y-intercept, the value of y when x is 0, essentially the line's starting point on the vertical axis, and m is the slope, which measures steepness as a rate of change: how much y changes for every one unit that x increases. Slope is calculated as rise over run, the change in y divided by the change in x, or in symbols, m = (y2 minus y1) divided by (x2 minus x1) for any two points on the line. A large positive slope means a steep upward line, a slope of zero means a flat horizontal line, and a negative slope means the line falls as you move right.

Suppose you know a line passes through the points (2, 3) and (5, 9), and you need its full equation. Start with slope: m equals (9 minus 3) divided by (5 minus 2), which is 6 divided by 3, or 2. Now use one point, say (2, 3), along with that slope in point slope form: y minus 3 equals 2 times (x minus 2). Distribute the 2: y minus 3 equals 2x minus 4. Add 3 to both sides, exactly the same balance-both-sides move from the previous chapter, and you get y equals 2x minus 1. Check it against both original points: at x = 2, y = 2(2) minus 1 = 3, correct, and at x = 5, y = 2(5) minus 1 = 9, correct.

Slope and intercept are not just abstract numbers, they describe real situations directly. If a taxi charges a flat $3 fee plus $2.50 per mile, the total cost follows y = 2.5x + 3, where the slope 2.50 is the rate charged per mile and the intercept 3 is the fixed cost before any miles are driven. Reading a linear equation this way, as a rate plus a starting amount, is exactly the skill the ACT tests in word problems, and it is also the exact shape of the functions you will meet in the next chapter, since y = mx + b is really just a function, f(x) = mx + b, wearing a different name.
